title: Tooth & Claw
desc: Predator tactics, survival extremes & the weirdest mating rituals on Earth

questions.q: The anglerfish has one of the most disturbing mating strategies in nature. What does the male do?
questions.a: He bites the female, fuses into her body, and slowly dissolves until he's nothing but a pair of gonads she can use when needed

questions.q: What is a 'zombie deer' and should we be worried?
questions.a: Deer infected with Chronic Wasting Disease (CWD) — a prion disease causing drooling, stumbling, and aggression. It hasn't jumped to humans yet, but scientists are watching it closely

questions.q: Why do some species of gecko lick their own eyeballs?
questions.a: They don't have eyelids — the tongue is their windscreen wiper, keeping the eye moist and clean

questions.q: The bombardier beetle defends itself by doing what?
questions.a: Firing a boiling chemical spray from its abdomen at 100°C — mixed internally from two separate chambers right before ejection

questions.q: What is the 'bloop' — the mysterious underwater sound detected by NOAA in 1997?
questions.a: Originally thought to be a massive unknown sea creature, it was later attributed to an icequake (ice cracking off an Antarctic glacier)

questions.q: Honey badgers are famously fearless. What's their actual defence mechanism that makes them so hard to kill?
questions.a: Extremely loose, thick skin — a predator that grabs them can't get a proper grip, and the badger can twist around inside its own skin to bite back
Still debated — theories include sonar interference from military exercises, magnetic navigation errors, illness, social bonds (following a sick leader), and parasitic brain infections

questions.q: The duck-billed platypus is venomous. Where is the venom delivered from?
questions.a: Spurs on the hind legs of males — the venom is excruciatingly painful to humans but not lethal

questions.q: What is 'biomimicry' and name one real-world invention inspired by nature?
questions.a: Designing technology by copying nature — Velcro (from burrs), bullet trains (from kingfisher beaks), wind turbines (from humpback whale fins)

questions.q: Trees in a forest cooperate through underground fungal networks — but they also wage chemical warfare against rivals. How?
questions.a: Some species release allelopathic chemicals from roots or falling leaves that inhibit competing plants' growth — black walnut trees are a classic example
